analysis.one_liner: Cuts excess federal subsidies to student loan holders and spends the savings on larger Pell Grants.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2004 with six Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate education committee, the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government guarantees student loans and pays loan holders an extra interest subsidy, called a special allowance, on top of what borrowers pay. Loans financed with tax-exempt bonds carried a higher 9.5% rate, and lenders could keep that premium rate on old loans — including loans made before 1993 — by repeatedly refinancing or transferring them. This bill would end the premium rate for loans that are refinanced, transferred, or refinanced after enactment, and would automatically put every dollar saved into raising the maximum Pell Grant, the main federal scholarship for low-income students. It was referred to the Senate education committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income college students, whose maximum Pell Grant would rise by an amount equal to the subsidy savings each year, and taxpayers, who would stop paying premium interest subsidies on old student loans that lenders have refinanced, transferred, or refinanced through other funding sources.

how_it_helps.text: It terminates the excess special allowance subsidy on covered loans — including old pre-1993 loans when they are refinanced, transferred, or financed by obligations that mature or are retired — by amending section 438(b)(2)(B) of the Higher Education Act.

It automatically appropriates, each fiscal year, an amount equal to the CBO-determined savings from the subsidy cut to increase the maximum Pell Grant, the main federal grant for low-income college students.

analysis.who_pays: Holders of federally guaranteed student loans — banks and other financial institutions in the Federal Family Education Loan Program — who would lose the higher special allowance rate on old loans when those loans are refinanced, financed by retired obligations, or sold or transferred.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the guaranteed special allowance could reduce loan holders' willingness to hold or finance federal student loans, and some state nonprofit lenders relied on the higher 9.5% yield to fund their lending operations, so the change carried a real risk to the supply of loan capital under the guaranteed-lender system.

The Pell Grant increase is not a permanent raise: each year's extra appropriation equals only that year's CBO-scored savings from the subsidy cut, so if the savings shrink or the mechanism is not renewed in later budget cycles, the grant boost does too.

The new lower subsidy rate applies only to loans originated, refinanced, financed, or transferred on or after enactment, so holders of untouched older loans would continue receiving the premium rate for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: dollars now going as guaranteed premium interest to loan holders would shift to Pell Grants for low-income students, with the amount set each year by CBO rather than by annual lobbying. The drawbacks are the normal risk of cutting guaranteed lender returns in a loan program that depends on lender participation, and the fact that the Pell increase exists only as long as the subsidy savings do. On balance, the design — pay for the student aid increase by closing a subsidy loophole rather than by adding new spending — is straightforward, and its main flaw is that it was never tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced at the end of September 2004 and sent to the Senate education committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in early January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Murray introduced the bill on September 29, 2004, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — after the September 29 referral.
The bill was never enacted; the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan holders kept collecting the higher special allowance on their older loans, and the potential Pell Grant increase never happened. No member of the public gained from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan holders kept the higher subsidy

against.name: Judd Gregg
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican in a Republican-run Senate without any floor action.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders and holders (banks and other FFEL program loan holders)
industries.note: These holders earn a federal special allowance payment on top of borrower interest, and loans financed with tax-exempt bonds carried a higher minimum yield — a rate lenders could keep collecting by repeatedly refinancing or transferring old loans, including pre-1993 loans. The bill ends the premium rate for covered loans and sends the savings to Pell Grants instead, so the industry's gain under the status quo comes directly at the expense of students and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Student loan secondary markets and tax-exempt bond financers
industries.note: Part of the 9.5% premium's value flowed to institutions that packaged and financed student loans through tax-exempt obligations; the bill cuts off the premium when a financing matures, is defeased, or the loan is refinanced or sold, reducing the payoff on that financing chain.
